title: The distribution of depressive symptoms by age, sex, and family type: A survey of school-going adolescents in Kampala, Uganda
content:
by Mellon Naijuka, Jane Namusoke, Nathaniel Mayengo, Henry Kibedi, Joseph Ssenyonga, Kennedy Amone-P’Olak

While depression in adolescents is known to be a public health concern and frequently related to poor psychosocial outcomes, little is known about its distribution, particularly in African countries like Uganda. This study assessed the prevalence, distribution, and odds of reporting depressive symptoms by age, sex, and in different family types in early adolescents. Using data from 347 young adolescents (12–15 years of age), we employed descriptive statistics, t-tests, and binary logistic regressions to calculate the odds of reporting depressive symptoms by age, sex, and in different family types: nuclear (reference), single-mother, mother and stepfather, father and stepmother, and relatives. Out of the 347 primary school-going adolescents aged between 12 and 15 years (Mean = 13.3, SD = 0.98, range 12–15), 173 were female (n = 173, 49.9%). About half of the respondents (n = 173, 49.9%) reported living in a nuclear family with both parents in the same household, while approximately 25% (n = 88) lived with a single mother. Overall, compared to the nuclear family type, the odds of reporting depressive symptoms for the single-mother family type and for adolescents living with relatives were 1.71 (95% Confidence Intervals (CI) 1.18, 2.36) and 1.76 (95% CI: 1.28, 2.48), respectively. The odds of reporting depressive symptoms are associated with being female, older (e.g., 15 years of age), living in a single-mother household, and with relatives. Interventions for early detection of vulnerable adolescents, particularly female and older adolescents, and those living in households with a high density of depressive symptoms should be prioritised.
